chunks: "The two common GPIO output types are push-pull and open-drain. Push-pull has a PMOS and an NMOS, so the pin actively drives both high and low.
Open-drain has only the NMOS: it can pull the line low, or let go, and then an external pull-up resistor pulls the line high. Push-pull wins on speed and power.
Both edges are driven by a low-impedance transistor, so the edges are fast, a few nanoseconds into a typical load, and no current flows when the pin is high.
It's the default for anything a single chip drives: LED enables, chip selects, SPI lines, UART TX. Open-drain wins on sharing and flexibility.
Several devices can connect to one wire without any danger of contention, because nobody ever drives high, so the line behaves as a wired-AND: any device can pull it low.
That's why I2C, shared interrupt lines and reset lines use it. The pull-up can also go to a different voltage, so it doubles as a simple level translator.
The costs are speed and power: the rising edge is an RC curve through the resistor, for 4.
7 kilohms and 100 picofarads that's about 400 nanoseconds, and every time the line is low it burns VDD over R, 0. 7 milliamps at 3. 3 volts. And you need the external resistor."
